items.prompt: An expense arrives with a well-formed body but a future date. Which layer rejects it, with which status?
distractors: DataAnnotations under [ApiController], as a malformed body: 400
The bearer-token authentication handler: 401
The [Authorize(Roles=...)] attribute on the action: 403
items.explanation: Shape problems are 400 from DataAnnotations; business rules such as 'no future date' are PolicyEngine flags answered with 422.

items.prompt: Approve carries [Authorize(Roles="Manager")]. Why does ExpenseService also call EnsureManagesOwner?
items.answer: The attribute only proves 'some manager'; the service check stops cross-team approvals
distractors: The attribute is skipped for API clients, so the service has to repeat the role check
EnsureManagesOwner refreshes the role claim if the token has expired
The service check only exists to write the approval into the audit history
items.explanation: Coarse attribute authorization is necessary but not sufficient; the resource check answers 'this manager manages this expense's owner'.

items.prompt: Someone adds UserRole.Auditor to the enum and nothing else. What can an Auditor see?
items.answer: Nothing: every role switch falls through to a deny arm
distractors: Everything an Employee can see, since that is the lowest existing role
Everything, because unknown roles are treated as administrators
Only their own expenses, via the owner-scoped GetOwned query
items.explanation: Every role switch has a `_ => false` / Enumerable.Empty arm: a new role gets no access until deliberately granted. The list of places to touch is the security surface.

items.prompt: Why can a blocking policy flag appear at submit time that was absent when the expense was created?
items.answer: Policy re-runs at create, update and submit on current data
distractors: Flags are only computed at submit; create and update skip the PolicyEngine entirely
The approver adds blocking flags by hand while reviewing the expense
A background job recalculates every flag nightly and stores the result
items.explanation: RefreshPolicy runs on each of the three operations; e.g. the stale-date warning depends on when it is evaluated.

items.prompt: How do Blocking and Warning flags from PolicyEngine differ in effect?
items.answer: Blocking flags stop submission; warnings travel with the expense to the approver
distractors: Blocking flags notify Finance; warnings are only written to the server log
Both stop submission, but the employee may override a warning
Warnings stop submission; blocking flags only show on the approver's screen
items.explanation: Rules include amount > 0, description present, no future date, receipt required over $25, per-category limits and a high-value warning.

items.prompt: The login path verifies a password hash to equalise timing, yet the guide calls that equalisation partial. Why?
items.answer: It still returns early when the user does not exist, so timing can differ
distractors: PBKDF2 with 100k iterations runs in variable time for different passwords
The constant-time comparison is only applied to the admin accounts
The salt is stored beside the hash, which leaks whether the user exists
items.explanation: PBKDF2 + per-user salt + constant-time compare is done right; the early return on a missing user is the gap to investigate.

items.prompt: Finance clicks reimburse; StartReimbursement flips the expense to Reimbursing and then enqueues the payment job. The process crashes before the worker dequeues it. What is the state after restart?
items.answer: Stuck in Reimbursing with no payment and nothing that will ever retry it
distractors: Back in Approved, because the unawaited enqueue never committed the status change
Reimbursed, because the bounded channel replays its pending jobs on startup
Paid twice, because the restart re-runs StartReimbursement for every Reimbursing expense
items.explanation: The status change happens first and the enqueue is neither awaited nor transactional; the queue is in-memory, so the job dies with the process and nothing recovers the expense.

items.prompt: The same ProcessReimbursement job runs twice for one expense. Why is the second run harmless?
items.answer: It re-checks CanSystemTransition, finds Reimbursed has no legal next edge, and returns
distractors: The bounded channel deduplicates identical delegates, so the second copy is never dequeued
It finds the existing PaymentReference and reuses it instead of issuing a new payment
QueuedHostedService catches the DomainException that Transition throws and drops the job
items.explanation: ProcessReimbursement is idempotent by guard: Reimbursed has no outgoing edge, so the legality re-check fails and it returns without paying again. ProcessReceipt has no such guard.

items.prompt: Moving from the singleton DataStore to a scoped, non-thread-safe DbContext, why is the background worker already structurally prepared?
items.answer: It opens a fresh DI scope per job, so each job can resolve its own scoped DbContext
distractors: Jobs run on the request thread, so they share the request's DbContext safely
The bounded channel runs one job at a time, so a singleton DbContext would be safe there
BackgroundService resolves every dependency as transient, so lifetimes never matter
items.explanation: DbContext must be scoped; code holding the store in a long-lived field would break, but the worker already calls CreateScope() per job, mimicking a per-request scope.

items.prompt: Mappings.ToResponse looks up the employee per expense with store.Users.GetValueOrDefault. Why does the guide call this current, harmless code a future bug?
items.answer: Under a real database, 100 expenses would fire 100 user lookups: an N+1
distractors: Users is a ConcurrentDictionary, so the lookup can return a torn read under load
It leaks the employee's password hash into the response DTO
GetValueOrDefault throws once an employee is deleted, failing the whole list response
items.explanation: In memory each lookup is a free dictionary hit; under EF Core each becomes a query. The fix is a join, Include or batch load.

items.prompt: The outbox redesign writes the status change and an OutboxEntry in one SaveChanges and lets a dispatcher perform the payment with retries. Why does the payment job still have to be idempotent?
items.answer: Delivery becomes at-least-once, so a crash-retry can run the payment twice
distractors: The outbox delivers exactly-once on its own; idempotency only matters for the receipt job
Idempotency replaces the transaction; with it the OutboxEntry could be written separately
The dispatcher runs on the request thread, so two requests can enqueue the same entry
items.explanation: The outbox converts at-most-once into at-least-once; at-least-once plus an idempotent side effect is what gives one payment, which the critique's test (kill the dispatcher mid-flight, restart, assert exactly-once payment) checks.

items.prompt: The background channel is full (capacity 100) when a request calls EnqueueAsync. What happens?
items.answer: The producer waits until the worker frees a slot
distractors: The oldest queued job is dropped to make room
EnqueueAsync throws immediately and the request returns 503
The channel grows past capacity and memory use rises without limit
items.explanation: BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait gives backpressure: producers wait instead of growing memory without limit.

items.prompt: Submit evaluates policy and then transitions, with no atomicity on a singleton in-memory store. What first step does the critique propose for the concurrency story?
items.answer: Document single-writer, add an optimistic-concurrency token; stale writes get 409
distractors: Wrap every service method in one global lock held around the whole DataStore singleton
Move policy evaluation into the background worker so it runs serially
Switch the store to a scoped lifetime so each request gets its own copy
items.explanation: R4 is a check-then-act gap (rare double-submit). The suggested start: state the assumption, add a concurrency token on Expense, reject stale writes; the test is two concurrent submits giving one 409.

items.front: Describe dotnet-ramp's two-layer authorization model for expenses (reads and writes).
items.back: Coarse: [Authorize(Roles=...)] says 'some manager'. Fine: service checks such as EnsureManagesOwner, CanView/List scoping reads to own/team/all by role, and owner-scoped writes via GetOwned. The fine layer is the IDOR defense.

items.front: Summarize the reliability properties of dotnet-ramp's in-process background queue.
items.back: In-memory, at-most-once: no durability (a crash loses queued and in-flight jobs), no retries, partial idempotency (ProcessReimbursement guards, ProcessReceipt does not), enqueue not transactional with the state change, visibility via logs only.

items.front: What five changes make dotnet-ramp's background processing production-grade?
items.back: Persist the queue (DB table or broker); an outbox for state-change-plus-side-effect atomicity; retry with backoff plus a dead-letter path; a stuck detector for Reimbursing older than N minutes; metrics for queue depth, job duration and failures.

items.front: How does the critique propose to test and roll back the reimbursement outbox?
items.back: An OutboxEntry is written in the same SaveChanges as the status change and polled by a dispatcher. Test: kill the dispatcher mid-flight, restart, assert exactly-once payment. Rollback: feature-flag the dispatcher and fall back to direct enqueue.
